hard_decisions: Hard decisions I don’t like to expose criminal activity against my sites, but when is annoying, I have no other choice. I really try to redirect attacks to my sites to this page, but after more than 1 week, I decided to redirect all attacks to some police service, while that is too strong, I decide to redirect them to my own GitHub repository. This decision is based on the false idea of having a lot of visit. KISS: Keep it Stupid Simple Click using the mouse, don’t try to use tools to attack this sites. There is nothing more than what is exposed: No Databases, No Users, No Emails, No dedicated-servers, etc.. Pure text, sometimes backgrounds and music. What the decision was not about It was not about revenge, and it was not about safety. Nobody who attacks a static page is going to be found, and nobody who runs a blog is going to become an investigator because of it. The decision was about attention: how much of my day belongs to a machine that was not invited. For a week I redirected the noise to a page that explains the attacks. The idea was generous, almost pedagogical: read what you are doing, maybe you will recognise yourself. It did not work, because the traffic that arrives is not looking at the page, it is looking at the answer code. Then the answer changed Redirecting to a police service would have been theatre, and theatre with consequences for nobody. Redirecting to my own repository is a smaller move with the same message: this is everything I have, it is public, and there is nothing behind the door you are trying to open. After that, the noise is still noise, but it is a noise I chose. That is the only part of the situation I can control, and controlling it was worth more than winning an argument with a script. The KISS of a static site No database means no injection. No users means no stolen passwords. No email list means no leak. No dedicated server means no server to compromise beyond a directory of files that any browser can download anyway. It is not a security architecture, it is the absence of one, and the absence is the point. The smaller the surface, the less there is to decide.

howAIworks: Neural Core Architecture Technical Specification & Processing Pipeline STATUS: ONLINE // READY FOR VECTOR STREAM Data Ingestion & Tokenization Before raw data can enter an artificial intelligence pipeline, unstructured input (text, images, audio) undergoes rigorous parsing. For Large Language Models (LLMs), text strings are split into discrete sub-word tokens using algorithms like Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) or WordPiece. Each token is mapped to an immutable integer index within a pre-defined vocabulary matrix $V$, typically containing between 32,000 to over 250,000 distinct tokens. Raw String: "Cyberpunk AI Core" Token Sequence: `["Cyber", "punk", " AI", " Core"]` Vocabulary IDs: `[14280, 18439, 9374, 5821]` # Python implementation of basic BPE Tokenization Simulation import re class SimpleTokenizer : def __init__ (self, vocab): self.vocab = vocab self.inv_vocab = {v: k for k, v in vocab.items()} def encode (self, text: str ) -> list : # Regex tokenizer partition tokens = re.findall( r'\w+|[^\w\s]' , text) return [self.vocab.get(t, 0 ) for t in tokens] # Execution Core vocab_map = { "Cyber" : 101 , "punk" : 102 , "AI" : 103 } tokenizer = SimpleTokenizer(vocab_map) token_ids = tokenizer.encode( "Cyber punk AI" ) print(token_ids) # Output: [101, 102, 103] Vectorization & Embeddings Integer IDs lack semantic meaning (e.g., token 500 isn't "greater" than token 100). The embedding layer transforms discrete token indices into continuous, high-dimensional dense vectors $\mathbb{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ (where dimension $d$ ranges from 768 to 12,800+). Furthermore, because transformers process inputs in parallel rather than sequentially, Positional Encodings or Rotary Embeddings (RoPE) are added directly to token vectors to encode word order and relative distance. $\mathbf{H}_0 = \text{Embedding}(X) + \text{PositionalEncoding}$ import torch import torch.nn as nn class EmbeddingPipeline (nn.Module): def __init__ (self, vocab_size, d_model): super ().__init__() self.token_embed = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model) self.pos_embed = nn.Embedding( 512 , d_model) def forward (self, input_ids): seq_len = input_ids.size( 1 ) positions = torch.arange( 0 , seq_len, device=input_ids.device) # Combine semantic and positional vectors out = self.token_embed(input_ids) + self.pos_embed(positions) return out Neural Network Forward Pass & Matrix Operations The core computational engine of modern deep learning relies on massive matrix multiplications (GEMM). At each linear layer, incoming activation tensors $\mathbf{X}$ are multiplied by weight matrices $\mathbf{W}$ and added to bias vectors $\mathbf{b}$. In attention mechanisms (Transformers), this expands into Query ($\mathbf{Q}$), Key ($\mathbf{K}$), and Value ($\mathbf{V}$) projections: $\text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)\mathbf{V}$ Hardware accelerators (GPUs/TPUs) parallelize these dot-product operations across thousands of streaming multiprocessors simultaneously. import math import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def scaled_dot_product_attention (Q, K, V): d_k = Q.size(- 1 ) # Matrix multiplication of Query and Transposed Key scores = torch.matmul(Q, K.transpose(- 2 , - 1 )) / math.sqrt(d_k) # Normalization via Softmax weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=- 1 ) # Final dot product with Value matrix return torch.matmul(weights, V), weights Activation Functions (ReLU / GELU) Linear transformations alone stack into a single linear operation. Activation functions introduce non-linearity, enabling artificial neural networks to approximate complex, non-linear functions (Universal Approximation Theorem). ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit): $\text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0, x)$. Computationally fast, prevents vanishing gradients for positive inputs. GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit): Weights inputs by their relative magnitude, widely used in modern transformer architectures like GPT and BERT. import torch import torch.nn as nn class CustomActivations : @staticmethod def relu (x): return torch.clamp(x, min= 0.0 ) @staticmethod def gelu (x): # Gaussian Error Linear Unit approximation return 0.5 * x * ( 1.0 + torch.tanh( math.sqrt( 2.0 / math.pi) * (x + 0.044715 * torch.pow(x, 3 )) )) Backpropagation & Gradient Descent During training, the model evaluates its prediction error against ground truth targets using a Loss Function (e.g., Cross-Entropy Loss). Backpropagation applies the chain rule of calculus in reverse order, calculating the partial derivative of the loss with respect to every weight parameter in the network ($\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}$). $\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \nabla_\theta L(\theta_t)$ Optimizers like AdamW use adaptive learning rates and momentum vectors to update weights efficiently across high-dimensional loss landscapes. import torch import torch.optim as optim # Dummy model and optimizer setup model = torch.nn.Linear( 10 , 2 ) optimizer = optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr= 1e-3 ) criterion = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss() # Training Step Iteration optimizer.zero_grad() # Clear stale gradients outputs = model(torch.randn( 4 , 10 )) loss = criterion(outputs, torch.tensor([ 1 , 0 , 1 , 0 ])) loss.backward() # Compute gradients via backprop optimizer.step() # Update weights via gradient descent Interactive Neural Architecture Simulation Simulate signal propagation through a deep neural network layer. hydroponics: Monkey Blog · Home Growing Home EN PT Home growing · a manual in sixteen parts Hydroponics at Home Roots in water instead of earth, a pump that keeps them breathing, and a nutrient solution you mix in a bucket. This manual takes that idea the whole way: six systems, the chemistry, the build you can make from what a city throws away, twelve steps from seed to plate, and the failures that kill a crop in a week. Six systems City-waste builds Water chemistry Seed to plate Portugal calendar Sources I want a first bucket this weekend Sections 01, 02 and 06, then the dated first month. Forty euros, one afternoon. I want to build it from waste Section 03: what is safe to reuse, six builds, what never goes near a reservoir. Something is dying Section 11: symptoms, the diagnosis order, pests, and what each leaf pattern means. I want to know what to sow now Section 08 opens on the current month, with a full Portuguese year behind it. 01 What a plant actually needs A plant does not eat soil. Soil holds the roots still, keeps them damp, lets air reach them and slowly releases minerals. Do those four jobs another way and the soil becomes optional — not magic, just one supplier among several. job 1 Support Net pots, clay pebbles, rockwool cubes or a foam collar hold the stem upright. A heavy fruit needs a string or a stake, not the pot. job 2 Water The solution reaches the roots continuously or in cycles. What soil did by capillarity, here a pump, a wick or a falling film does. job 3 Oxygen Roots respire. Wet roots without air suffocate in days, which is why every system that works either moves the water or bubbles air through it. job 4 Minerals Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and the trace elements arrive dissolved and measured, instead of waiting to be released by soil life. The honest ledger Hydroponics is a tool for space, control and clean water — not an automatic claim to sustainability. The trade is specific, and it is worth knowing before you buy anything. What you gain 70–90 % less water than the same crop in open soil, because nothing drains away. No weeds, no soil-borne pests, no digging, no backache. Growth is faster when light and oxygen are right — often two or three weeks per cycle. The garden moves with you: indoors in November, balcony in April. You see the plant's food. EC and pH are a dashboard no soil grower gets. What you pay for it A pump or power failure is fatal within hours in warm weather — the roots have no reservoir of soil. Water chemistry becomes your job, and mistakes show up as leaf edges two weeks later. Energy: a controlled-environment study found lettuce yields 11× higher per area but 82× the energy per head, mostly lighting. Plastic, salts and meters are consumables; a system is a small appliance, not a closed loop. You buy the nutrients. Compost does not dissolve, and manure tea does not belong in a recirculating reservoir. The one-line version: hydroponics replaces soil with plumbing, and plumbing fails loudly. It is at its best where soil is impossible — a fourth-floor flat, a dark January, a balcony with 0.4 m² — and at its worst as a promise that it will save money. 02 Six systems, one ladder Six ways to keep roots wet and breathing. They are ordered by how much can go wrong, not by how impressive they look: start at the top and move down only when a plant — not boredom — gives you the reason. Start here: Kratky, or a wick No electricity, no timer, no noise. Lettuce, basil, rocket, pak choi. If this fails, the cause is temperature or light, and you learn it for €5. Then: one deep-water bucket Add an air pump and a 20 L reservoir and you can grow a tomato. The pump is the first thing that can break, and the first thing worth learning to hear. Then: drip or a channel A timer, emitters, a return line: this is where a home system starts to behave like a small machine and needs a weekly inspection, not a glance. Only if you must: aeroponics The fastest growth and the shortest grace period. A clogged nozzle kills a crop before lunch. Run it beside a bucket, never instead of one. Kratky DWC NFT Drip Aeroponics Wick best first system Kratky — passive, no pump, no electricity A jar, a net pot, nutrient solution. The roots drink, the level drops, an air gap forms and the upper roots breathe it. Nothing moves, nothing hums. Lettuce, basil, rocket, pak choi: one plant per 1–3 litre jar, 4–6 weeks. watch out Limits Water temperature decides everything: above 24 °C the solution runs out of oxygen and root rot starts. Not for tomatoes or anything that lives four months. Change the solution every two weeks; never top up to the brim once roots hang in the air gap. the workhorse Deep water culture — bucket, lid, air stone 10–20 litres in a bucket, an aquarium air pump with a stone, roots permanently submerged and constantly oxygenated. Fast growth, forgiving of a missed top-up, and the cheapest way to grow a real tomato plant indoors. watch out Details Keep the water at 18–22 °C — a black bucket in the sun will cook it; wrap it in foil or paint it white. One 3–5 W pump per two buckets is enough. If the pump stops for a day in summer, the plant may not survive. for many small plants Nutrient film technique — a shallow stream in a channel A pump lifts solution to one end of a tilted pipe; a 2–3 mm film runs past the roots and drains back into the tank. Excellent for 20 lettuce heads on a shelf, poor for fruit: the channel is too small for a big root ball. watch out Details A blocked channel starves a whole row in an hour. Slope 1–2 %, never more. Filter the return, and check flow daily in hot weather. for fruit Drip — a pot of pebbles, watered on a timer Each plant sits in clay pebbles; a small pump drips solution onto the pot three to six times a day and it drains back to the tank. The standard way to grow tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, strawberries and herbs from one shared reservoir. watch out Details Emitters clog with nutrient salts — clean them monthly in warm water. Because the reservoir is shared, one sick plant spreads to all: inspect roots weekly. advanced Aeroponics — roots in air, misted Roots hang in a closed box; nozzles spray a fine mist every few minutes. The highest oxygen levels of any method and the fastest growth — and the least tolerant of failure: a clogged nozzle means dead roots in hours. watch out Details Needs a timer with seconds, a filter, and a spare pump. Do not start here. If you want the experiment, run it beside a DWC so one crop survives. simplest possible Wick — a cord does the pumping A cotton or nylon cord runs from a reservoir into a pot of pebbles or coco coir and pulls solution up by capillarity. Good for herbs, lettuce and a windowsill, and it cannot flood the roots. watch out Details Weak flow limits big plants, and the cord clogs with salts after a month or two — replace it. Coco coir buffers the pH and hides the water, so check the reservoir weekly rather than the surface. The same six, side by side Cost is for the first build in Portugal, late 2026; failure mode is what happens when the power goes out in July. System Moving parts Cost Best crop When it fails Choosing by what you want to eat Start from the plate, not from the catalogue What you want System Floor space Effort Salad and herbs for one person Kratky jars or wick 0.2 m² Minutes a week Lettuce every week NFT channel or DWC 0.5–1 m² Weekly top-up Tomatoes, peppers, cucumber DWC buckets or drip 1–2 m² Twice a week Strawberries Drip or wide NFT channels 0.5 m² Twice a week Microgreens Shallow tray, no system at all 0.1 m² Every 2 days 03 Build it from the city's waste Every reservoir in this manual can be bought new for forty euros, or found for nothing. A city produces exactly the containers a hydroponic garden needs — food-grade drums, bakery crates, pipes, shelving — and throws most of them away after one use. The skill is not finding them. It is knowing which ones are safe. Why reuse beats recycling. A kilo of new HDPE carries roughly 1.8–2 kg of CO₂e before it holds a drop of water; a 20-litre drum weighs about a kilo. Reusing it saves the material, the moulding energy and the €6 — while recycling it saves only part of the first. The EU's own hierarchy puts prevention and reuse above recycling, and the plastics strategy is built on that order. A garden that buys new plastic every season is not circular, whatever the bucket is made of. The rule that matters more than the number The little triangle tells you the polymer. It does not tell you what the container held, who made it, or what was added to it. History beats code: a #2 drum that carried screen wash is scrap, and a #5 tub that carried yoghurt is a seedling pot after one wash. Buy nothing that ever held a biocide, a solvent, a fuel, a paint or anything whose label you cannot read. The seven resin codes, as they apply to a reservoir — not to a bottle of water Code Polymer Where you find it For a reservoir Clean it like a vessel, not like a dish A used container carries two things you cannot see: the residue of what it held, and a biofilm that will feed algae and root rot. Five steps, forty minutes, once per container. Strip the label and the glue Warm water with a spoon of bicarbonate, or a little cooking oil on the adhesive. Solvents are not worth the risk on something that will hold plant food. Scrub, do not soak Hot water, washing-up liquid, a brush that reaches the corners. Rinse until the water runs clear and no foam remains. Never use a scouring pad on the inside of a reservoir: the scratches become a permanent home for biofilm. Sanitise with dilute bleach One part thin household bleach (about 5 %) to nine parts water, ten minutes of contact, then two full rinses. Three per cent hydrogen peroxide works too, at 3 ml per litre, with no rinse needed. Never mix bleach with an acid — including pH-down. Bleach plus acid releases chlorine gas. Dry it in the sun Ultraviolet light is free disinfectant. An hour upside down on a balcony does more than a second wash. Store dry, lid off, so it cannot grow a smell. Test the rinse water Fill with clean water, stir, read the EC. If it climbs above 0.1 mS/cm, something is still dissolving out of the plastic. Rinse again, or demote the container to holding pebbles. Five builds, from a bottle to a tote Each is a complete, working system. The dimensions are the ones that fit a windowsill or a balcony in a Portuguese flat; scale them, do not shrink them — a reservoir that is too small is the most common reason a build fails in August. build 1 · €0–3 · 20 minutes The 5-litre bottle Kratky One bottle, one net pot, one lettuce. The cheapest honest test of whether you enjoy this. A 5 L PET water bottle, label off, top cut at the shoulder A net pot that sits in the neck, or a plastic cup with holes Clay pebbles, or washed gravel A seedling in a rockwool cube or a plug Wrap the bottle in paper or paint it: clear plastic grows algae in a week. Fill with solution to about a third, EC 0.8, pH 5.8. Seat the plant so the cube's bottom just touches the liquid. Never top up to the brim. The air gap that forms as the level drops is what the upper roots breathe. One crop per bottle: PET softens in sun and holds smells. Refill once, then recycle it and start a new one. build 2 · €12 new, €0 found · one afternoon The 20-litre drum DWC The workhorse. Two lettuce, or one tomato, with an air stone and a lid you can cut. A 20 L HDPE drum: a food bucket from a bakery, or a jerry can from a car wash An aquarium air pump, 2–3 W, with stone and 1 m of tube Two 8 cm net pots and 3 L of clay pebbles A lid, or a piece of rigid foam board cut to size Cut two holes in the lid, 8 cm, spaced as far apart as the drum allows. Drill a 6 mm notch for the air tube at the rim, not through the lid's middle. Fill to 2 cm below the pots, start the pump, and check for bubbles before planting. Wrap the drum in an old rice sack: it keeps light out and heat down for nothing. Food buckets from bakeries held mayonnaise, olives or pickles — safe after the wash. A drum that held engine oil never becomes a reservoir, whatever you clean it with. build 3 · €15 new, €5 found · for 6–10 plants The gutter or crate NFT A length of gutter, a bakery crate with a liner, or a plastic cable tray: anything that holds a 2 mm film and slopes. 2 m of PVC or PP gutter, with two end caps A 10 L tank and a 5 W submersible pump Net pots, 5 cm, one per 20 cm A lid or black membrane to keep light off the film Set the channel on two bricks: 2 cm of fall over 2 m is 1 %, which is enough. Feed at the high end through a 4 mm tube; drain at the low end through a bulkhead or a drilled cap. Cut pot holes 20 cm apart and cover the rest of the channel with a lid. Run the pump continuously for lettuce; five minutes on, fifteen off for herbs. Old PVC gutters can contain lead stabilisers and are a poor choice for edible crops. Prefer new PP, or a food crate with a food-grade liner. build 4 · €20–40 found · a balcony or a yard The IBC tote, cut in half A 1000 L IBC that carried juice or syrup is the best free reservoir a city offers: food-grade HDPE, a steel cage, and a tap already fitted. One 1000 L IBC, food-grade, with its cage and pallet A saw, a file, and gloves A submersible pump and 13 mm hose Net pots and pebbles for the raft, or six pots for drip Cut it a third from the top: the shallow part becomes a raft bed, the deep part a reservoir. File every edge — a cut IBC is a blade. Wear gloves, not sandals. Drill an overflow 3 cm below the raft's rim and plumb it back to the reservoir. Float a foam board with 5 cm holes: lettuce and basil on top, water underneath. A full 1000 L tote weighs a tonne. Put it on a ground-floor terrace or over a load-bearing wall, never on a balcony slab without checking what it was designed for. build 5 · €0 · five minutes The wick tub, for herbs and a north window Two tubs stacked, one wick, no electricity. The one system that survives a fortnight away. A 1 L yoghurt tub with its lid, plus a second tub as the reservoir A strip of old cotton T-shirt, 3 cm wide and 20 cm long Coco coir or pebbles, and a herb seedling Cut a slot in the upper tub's base and thread the cotton through, 5 cm inside. Fill the lower tub with solution, set the upper tub inside so the wick dips. Plant into the coir, water once from above, and leave it. Replace the wick every two months: it clogs with salts and stops lifting water. Wicks suit basil, mint, parsley and lettuce. They cannot deliver enough water for a tomato in July. Where a city keeps its parts Ask once, in person, and most of these become a weekly supply. Nobody at a bakery is attached to the bucket the mayonnaise came in. Twelve sources, what to ask for, and the catch Source Ask for Becomes Catch Never in a reservoir, whatever the label says: Anything that held oil, fuel, antifreeze, screen wash, paint, solvent, pesticide or a cleaning product. Plastic absorbs; rinsing does not undo it. Black recycled plastic from electronics, for anything that touches solution. It is often e-waste derived and can carry flame retardants. Galvanised steel, copper, brass or zinc fittings in contact with the solution — zinc and copper are toxic to roots at surprisingly low levels. Old PVC pipe or vinyl hose for edible crops; historic lead stabilisers are the reason it is avoided in drinking-water plumbing. Treated, painted or unknown timber, and pallets stamped MB (methyl bromide). HT, heat-treated, is the one to take. Tyres, polystyrene fish boxes and anything that smells of its last contents after two washes. About microplastics, honestly. Every plastic reservoir sheds a little, and warm, slightly acidic nutrient solution is a mildly aggressive environment. Choose HDPE or PP over PET, keep the tank out of the sun, do not scrub the inside, and replace anything cracked or chalky. The World Health Organization found no evidence of harm from microplastics in drinking water at current levels, and your lettuce is not drinking it — but "no evidence of harm" is not the same as "no plastic", and a glass jar is still the better choice for a windowsill. 04 Water is the medium In soil, water is an ingredient. Here it is the room the roots live in, so its temperature, its hardness and what your municipality put in it all become part of the recipe. Four sources, in the order a city dweller should consider them. the best one Rain from your own roof Nearly zero EC, no chlorine, free. One millimetre of rain on one square metre of roof is one litre; forty square metres of roof in Lisbon collect about 25 000 litres a year, which is a hundred times what a small system drinks. the default Tap water Perfectly usable. Let it stand 12–24 hours for chlorine, or neutralise chloramine with 50 mg of ascorbic acid per 10 litres. Read its EC before you add anything: that number is your floor. the free bonus Condensate from an air conditioner A working split unit in a Portuguese summer produces litres a day at almost zero EC. Fine for topping up a reservoir; not for drinking, and not for an aeroponic mister, where the aerosol is inhaled. with a caveat Water from an aquarium Mild nutrients and living microbes — excellent for a wick pot or the soil garden, risky in a sterile recirculating system where you cannot see what is blooming. Never pour it into a shared reservoir. Catching rain without making a mess A downpipe, a first-flush diverter, a filter and an opaque tank with a mosquito screen. The first two litres off a dry roof carry bird droppings and dust — discard them. Keep the tank dark: light grows algae, and an algae tank costs you more in pH swings than the water saved. On a balcony, a 100–200 L barrel under a downpipe is enough for a small system and a few pots, and it weighs 200 kg when full, so put it over a wall, not over the neighbour. Hard water. If your tap starts above EC 0.6, part of the reading is calcium and magnesium you did not add. Use rain or filtered water, or subtract the tap reading from the target and feed the difference. Never chase EC 3.0 with water that already sits at 1.0 without watching the leaf tips for burn. Temperature is oxygen Warm water holds less oxygen, and roots burn through oxygen faster when it is warm. This is the single number that decides whether a passive system lives through August. Keep the solution under 24 °C, and treat 26 °C as an alarm. Oxygen saturation of fresh water at sea level, and what it means for roots Water °C O₂ saturation mg/L What happens 15 10.1 Comfortable. Lettuce grows without complaint. 20 9.1 The target range for most home systems. 24 8.4 The line. Add air, shade the tank, or both. 28 7.8 Warm, oxygen-poor, and where root rot begins. 30 7.6 Emergency: chill, shade, increase flow, or harvest early. Roots want at least 5 mg/L of dissolved oxygen, which is why an air stone is not optional in deep water culture. A frozen 1.5 L bottle dropped into the tank in the evening buys a hot afternoon; a white or foil-wrapped tank buys the whole summer; a pump that runs at night buys the margin between the two. 05 Nutrients and the only two numbers pH and EC. One says whether the food is available, the other says how much food is there. Two meters cost about €30 together, and they replace every guess in this manual. Target ranges by crop (mS/cm = EC; 1 mS/cm ≈ 500–700 ppm depending on the meter's scale) Crop pH EC mS/cm Days to harvest Litres / plant pH: the lock on the cupboard Most crops want pH 5.5–6.5. Below 5.5 calcium and magnesium lock up; above 6.5 iron does. Adjust downwards with phosphoric or citric acid, upwards with potassium bicarbonate — a few drops at a time, stirring between each, because the response is not linear. Then measure again 24 hours later: drift is normal, a jump of more than 0.5 in a day means too little water or too much plant. EC: the strength of the soup EC measures total dissolved salts, not a nutrient. It cannot tell nitrogen from sodium. That is why you measure it
i3Hero: ↶ Home Field Manual I3H-1 · a WM that obeys, one line at a time i3 Desktop — From Nothing to Hero The tiling window manager that fits in one config file and one head. This page is the road from a bare X session to a desk that is yours: the config file, the keys, workspaces, the bar, icons that actually render, the extra software that glues a desktop together, and a complete annotated fancy config — every value explained by the line that sets it. config · workspaces · glyphs · rofi · picom vanilla JS · CSS3 · no dependencies every value reversible, one line at a time 01 From nothing i3 is a tiling window manager for X11, created by Michael Stapelberg and friends, with two rare virtues among WMs: it is complete without a desktop environment , and it is configured entirely in one text file that you can read, version and print. Nothing is hidden behind a GUI settings tool — that is not a limitation, it is the whole culture. Tiling by default: windows share the screen instead of covering each other. The mouse survives for exactly two jobs — resizing and clicking sometimes. Keyboard-driven by contract: $mod (usually Super ) plus a letter does everything. Stable where it matters: the IPC protocol and the config language have stayed compatible for over a decade; configs from 2012 still work in 2026. Siblings of the family: i3blocks , i3lock , i3status , and the Wayland rewrite sway (same config language). $ apt install i3 i3lock i3status # or pkg / dnf / pacman equivalents $ echo "exec i3" > ~/.xinitrc $ startx # or pick i3 at your display manager's login First launch runs i3-config-wizard : it writes a starter config and asks one question that matters for the rest of your life — your Super / Alt preference for $mod , plus how you want Win -key alternatives laid out. Choose Super : Alt belongs to the applications Emacs, Firefox and everything in between. Note: the wizard's output is just a normal config file. Everything it wrote can be re-edited by hand from now on, and this page assumes ~/.config/i3/config (or ~/.i3/config , whose existence it still honours as a fallback). 02 The configuration file One file: ~/.config/i3/config . Plain text, one directive per line, # for comments. There are no plugins, no modules, no scripts inside — which is why you never fear a typo breaking half of your desktop at once. Directive Means set $mod Mod4 Name a key once, use it everywhere ( Mod4 = Super , Mod1 = Alt ). bindsym Bind one key combo to an action or a command ( bind gives named modes with fallbacks). exec / exec_always Run a program at startup; exec_always also reruns on i3 restart . assign / for_window Send new windows to workspaces / apply rules to matching windows (criteria in [brackets] ). bar { } The block that defines the whole bar (position, status command, colours, tray). set_from_resource Read a value from X resources before falling back to a literal (nice for theming). # ~/.config/i3/config — smallest honest start (numbers in comments explain lines) set $mod Mod4 # 01: Super is the leader key set $term xterm # 02: one terminal variable, used everywhere below bindsym $mod+Return exec $term # 03 bindsym $mod+Shift+q kill # 04 bindsym $mod+h split h # 05 bindsym $mod+v split v # 06 bindsym $mod+j focus down # 07 bindsym $mod+k focus up # 08 bindsym $mod+Shift+j move down # 09 bindsym $mod+Shift+k move up # 10 bindsym $mod+1 workspace 1 # 11: one line per workspace bindsym $mod+2 workspace 2 bindsym $mod+Shift+c reload # 12: re-read the config, keep windows bindsym $mod+Shift+r restart # 13: restart i3 entirely bindsym $mod+Shift+e exec "i3-nagbar -t warning -m 'Exit i3?' -B 'Yes' 'i3-msg exit'" The two reload commands are different and worth knowing early: reload re-reads the config into the running session; restart replaces the WM process itself — the reason an X restart is rarely needed to fix WM problems. Note: i3-msg is the command-line twin of the keys: run i3-msg workspace 3 from a shell to switch workspaces, i3-msg 'resize grow width 40 px' to poke the layout from scripts or i3-nagbar . i3 --moreversion also tells you at a glance if you broke something with the config when i3 refuses a reload. 03 Keys first, mouse optional The key grammar is one verb family: focus , move , workspace , layout , resize , mark . Learn it once and it survives any monitor arrangement: Chord Action The sentence it writes $mod+d exec dmenu_run A launcher appears; type to run anything installed. $mod+w / $mod+s / $mod+e layout tabbed / stacking / toggle split Each container cycles between the three layouts. $mod+f / $mod+Shift+space fullscreen toggle / floating toggle Escape hatches when a tiling assumption breaks. $mod+space focus mode_toggle Move focus between tiled and floating windows. $mod+r resize (mode) Enter the built-in resize arrows mode; same keys again to leave. $mod+Shift+s sticky toggle sticky flag Floating window follows you across workspaces. $mod+a / $mod+Shift+a focus parent / focus child Walk the container tree instead of hashtables of corners. Note: bindsym binds the keysym; bindcode binds keycodes and survives layout switches on non-English keyboards. If your national characters break bindsym bindings, switch those specific binds to bindcode with xev to find the code. 04 Workspaces and layout Workspaces are i3's answer to virtual desktops: ten of them by default, bound to $mod+1..10 and named whatever you like (icons in section 07 use names, not numbers): set $ws1 "1: term" set $ws2 "2: web" set $ws10 "10: mail" bindsym $mod+1 workspace $ws1 bindsym $mod+2 workspace $ws2 bindsym $mod+Shift+2 move container to workspace $ws2 Layout is a tree. Each workspace holds containers ; each container splits horizontally/vertically, or switches to tabbed/stacking. The tree is why: $mod+e (toggle split) flips the last container's split direction — the "swap two windows' arrangement" trick. $mod+a then $mod+v / $mod+h changes where the next window appears : focus parent first, then split — the honest way to do “open my editor below my browser inside workspace 2”. $mod+Shift+1..10 moves a window to another workspace, and with $mod+Shift+space first it can float instead. # window rules on the tree (for_window + criteria) for_window [class="^xfce4-notes"] floating enable assign [class="^ Firefox$"] $ws2 assign [class="^thunderbird\ "] $ws10 Note: find the exact class / title strings with xprop (click the window): WM_CLASS(STRING) is what criteria use. Guess never; everyone who guesses ends up with rules that match the wrong window. 05 Starting things automatically i3 has one startup mechanism and no autostart daemon folklore: /etc/i3/config exec lines (yours, in ~/.config/i3/config ). exec --no-startup-id nm-applet # network tray applet exec --no-startup-id picom -b # compositor, daemon mode (section 10) exec --no-startup-id dunst # notifications server exec_always --no-startup-id feh --bg-scale ~/Pictures/wall.jpg exec --no-startup-id xss-lock --transfer-sleep-lock --i3lock --nofork Two honesty points: --no-startup-id stops i3 from grabbing focus for the started window — desktops lose their minds less when this flag is used. That is all of it. No ~/.config/autostart , no XFCE daemons, no systemd user units required here. If a program refuses to start this way (an updater that insists) put it in your ~/.xprofile file instead; but the config is where desk-startup belongs. Note: the xss-lock line is the sane way to wire i3lock to suspend: the screen locks itself before the laptop sleeps, so the password prompt is waiting when the lid opens. 06 The bar, without tears i3's built-in bar is driven by the bar { } block in the config and a status command that prints one line of text: i3status by default, i3blocks or polybar when you outgrow it. bar { position top status_command i3status -c ~/.config/i3/i3status.conf tray_output primary font pango:JetBrainsMono Nerd Font 10 separator_symbol " | " colors { background #0b110d statusline #eef4f0 separator #9aaf9e focused_workspace #9fe870 #1f3a24 #0b110d active_workspace #4d6b52 #16241a #9aaf9e inactive_workspace #16241a #0b110d #5f7a63 urgent_workspace #ff9d5c #3a241f #0b110d } } And a minimal ~/.config/i3/i3status.conf to feed it: general { interval = 5 colors = true } order += "wireless _first_" order += "ethernet _first_" order += "battery all" order += "load" order += "time" wireless _first_ { format_up = "%quality %essid" format_down = "" } ethernet _first_ { format_up = "%ip" format_down = "" } battery all { format = "%status %percentage %remaining" } time { format = "%H:%M:%S" } Note: i3blocks swaps the INI above for a set of little scripts named by block; anything that can print a line to stdout can be a block. That model, plus glyph fonts (next section), is where a laptop bar stops being a battery line and starts being a dashboard. 07 Icons that render i3 has no icon system of its own — the only “icons” on an i3 desk are glyphs in a font , used in three places: workspace names, status blocks, and per-window titles ( for_window rules). The one prerequisite is a font that actually contains the glyphs: $ apt install fonts-noto fonts-jetbrains-mono fonts-nerd-fonts-meta # or the classic trinity: fonts-font-awesome, ttf-nerd-fonts-symbols, fonts-emojione $ fc-list | grep -i "nerd\|awesome" # confirm the family name you will type in configs Then the font name (exact, from fc-list ) becomes the config currency: # everywhere in the WM — the exact family name from fc-list, not a guess: font pango:JetBrainsMono Nerd Font 10 # workspace names carry their glyphs directly (Unicode code points): set $ws1 "1: term" set $ws2 "2: " bindsym $mod+1 workspace $ws1 # and per-app window titles can too: for_window [class="Firefox"] title_format "2: %title" Some of the most useful code points, from a Nerd Font / Font Awesome at their conventional places (your fc-list family decides how they look, not the config):  house  laptop  battery  wifi  volume  code  globe  mail  tv  wrench Note: both i3status and i3blocks print these glyphs straight out of shell scripts — the block script's stdout is the bar. UTF-8 in, bar out; no plugin layer, no daemon to restart (well: killall -USR1 i3blocks if you swap scripts live, or plain restart which everyone does instead). Warn: if a glyph shows as a box, the family name in font pango:... does not match fc-list exactly — case, hyphen and last word all count ( Nerd Font , not NerdFonts ; Font Awesome 6 Free , not FontAwesome6 ). The fix is always in one place: the font line. 08 Extra software that glues the desk An i3 install is deliberately naked. The extras below are what turn it from a WM into a desk, with the role each one plays in one sentence: Tool Fills One-line install shape rofi dmenu's GTK-styled cousin: launcher, window switcher and much more with themes bindsym $mod+d exec rofi -show drun picom Compositor: shadows, transparency, vsync, no screen tearing exec --no-startup-id picom -b -c dunst Notification daemon for real (dbus) notifications exec --no-startup-id dunst feh / nitrogen Wallpaper setter (feh is the scripted one) exec_always --no-startup-id feh --bg-fill ~/w.png i3lock Screen lock, with colour or blur background bindsym $mod+Shift+x exec i3lock -c 000000 maim / scrot Screenshots (selection / whole screen) bindsym Print exec maim -s ~/shot.png network-manager-applet Wifi/network in the tray + password prompts exec --no-startup-id nm-applet pavucontrol Per-app volume when hotkeys are not enough bindsym $mod+F11 exec pavucontrol autorandr Remembers monitor layouts per physical arrangement exec --no-startup-id autorandr --change xss-lock Ties lock/suspend together exec --no-startup-id xss-lock -- i3lock -c 000000 The glue lines most desks end up wanting, exactly as written: # volume keys, PulseAudio flavour (swap pactl for amixer on pure ALSA boxes) bindsym XF86AudioRaiseVolume exec --no-startup-id pactl set-sink-volume @DEFAULT_SINK@ +5% bindsym XF86AudioLowerVolume exec --no-startup-id pactl set-sink-volume @DEFAULT_SINK@ -5% bindsym XF86AudioMute exec --no-startup-id pactl set-sink-mute @DEFAULT_SINK@ toggle # brightness (libinput-backed laptops use the sysfs path; check `ls /sys/class/backlight/`) bindsym XF86MonBrightnessUp exec --no-startup-id brightnessctl set +5% bindsym XF86MonBrightnessDown exec --no-startup-id brightnessctl set 5%- Note: keep one launcher only. People who bind dmenu on $mod+d and rofi on $mod+r end up searching two lists to find one app. Pick rofi (or pick nothing); one door is a desk, two doors is a puzzle. Warn: picom with experimental_backends = true was the classic tearing fix, but with vsync mis-set it becomes the tear cause. If frames stutter after enabling any compositor, the first suspect is its vsync: honest options are vsync = true (OpenGL) or no — not both worlds at once. 09 The fancy config, annotated Here is the target: one dark, gap-using, rofi-launched, notification-served i3 with iconed workspaces and a themed bar — every value explained by the comment on its line. This is meant to be read top to bottom ; every number is a real knob. # ~/.config/i3/config — the fancy build, annotated by line # --- identity ---------------------------------------------------------------- set $mod Mod4 # Super; swap to Mod1 if your desk prefers Alt set $term xterm # every exec below uses $term: change once set $menu rofi -show drun # theme lives in ~/.config/rofi/config.rasi font pango:JetBrainsMono Nerd Font 10 # the one font line the whole WM reads # --- the essential keys ------------------------------------------------------ bindsym $mod+Return exec $term bindsym $mod+d exec $menu bindsym $mod+Shift+q kill bindsym $mod+Shift+c reload bindsym $mod+Shift+r restart bindsym $mod+Shift+e exec "i3-nagbar -t warning -m 'You pressed exit shortcut. Do you really want to exit i3?' -B 'Yes, exit i3' 'i3-msg exit'" # --- focus, like arrows on tilers -------------------------------------------- bindsym $mod+j focus down bindsym $mod+k focus up bindsym $mod+h focus left bindsym $mod+l focus right # vim keys as well, free at the same bindings: bindsym $mod+Shift+j move down bindsym $mod+Shift+k move up bindsym $mod+Shift+h move left bindsym $mod+Shift+l move right # --- splits and layouts ------------------------------------------------------ bindsym $mod+b split h bindsym $mod+v split v bindsym $mod+f fullscreen toggle bindsym $mod+s layout stacking bindsym $mod+w layout tabbed bindsym $mod+e layout toggle split bindsym $mod+space focus mode_toggle # --- workspaces with glyphs, one block each ---------------------------------- set $ws1 "1: " # term set $ws2 "2: " # web set $ws3 "3: " # code set $ws4 "4: " # mail set $ws10 "10: " # settings bindsym $mod+1 workspace $ws1 bindsym $mod+2 workspace $ws2 bindsym $mod+3 workspace $ws3 bindsym $mod+4 workspace $ws4 bindsym $mod+0 workspace $ws10 bindsym $mod+Shift+1 move container to workspace $ws1 bindsym $mod+Shift+2 move container to workspace $ws2 # --- windows and rules ------------------------------------------------------- gaps inner 10 # i3 ≥ 4.24 (gaps merge) or i3-gaps: the breathing quantity gaps outer 4 smart_gaps on # no gaps when a single window fills the screen default_border pixel 2 # 1-2px: WM chrome you barely see but always find default_floating_border pixel 2 hide_edge_borders smart focus_follows_mouse no # focus by keys is a decision, not a hover accident Read it again with the annotations: nothing above is magic; it is all one concept per line . The full file for a working laptop also merges the sections below — bar block, startup execs, keyranges for volume — and lands around 120 lines; not 1200. The $menu variable exists to prove the launcher slot can take any command string — swap it and the desk keeps its keys. Note: keep the file in git. An i3 config repo earns its keep faster than any dotfile: a bad weekend of tweak-fu is undone by git checkout ~/.config/i3/config , not by memory. 10 Gaps, borders and transparency The fancy layer has exactly three ingredients, two of which live in the config and one lives in a separate program: # colours: focused vs. the world (borders + text pairs) client.focused #9fe870 #16241a #eef4f0 #9fe870 #9fe870 client.focused_inactive #4d6b52 #16241a #9aaf9e #4d6b52 #4d6b52 client.unfocused #16241a #0b110d #5f7a63 #16241a #16241a client.urgent #ffb38a #3a241f #0b110d #ffb38a #ffb38a client.placeholder #16241a #0b110d #9aaf9e #16241a #16241a Each meaning is the same 5-part colour list: border · background · text · indicator · child_border . Setting client.focused is how a desk says “this is the window I am inside” visually — the strongest single upgrade after the font. # transparency comes from picom's config, not from i3: # ~/.config/picom/picom.conf opacity-rule = [ "95:class_g = 'URxvt'", "100:class_g = 'firefox'" ] shadow = true shadow-radius = 14 vsync = true # the bool that rules tearing; one of its two values is honest Warn: screens look smoother with transparency, but every transparent window costs a composite. On battery-starved hardware the optional picom is the correct answer; a desk is not a benchmark of compositors. 11 The scratchpad and resize mode The scratchpad is i3's best-kept secret: a floating window that can hide and pop on any workspace. One terminal on it, summoned anywhere, is the toy desktops tend to stop rebuilding around: # make-move-toggle ritual, bound once, used forever bindsym $mod+Shift+minus move scratchpad # send the focused floating window to it bindsym $mod+minus scratchpad show # summon/cycle scratchpad windows exec --no-startup-id $term -name scratch for_window [instance="scratch"] move scratchpad, scratchpad show, resize set 90 ppt 35 ppt for_window [instance="scratch"] floating enable, sticky enable, border pixel 2 And resize mode , i3's own modal gem — $mod+r turns arrow keys into resize keys until Escape : mode "resize" { bindsym h resize shrink width 10 px or 5 ppt bindsym l resize grow width 10 px or 5 ppt bindsym k resize shrink height 10 px or 5 ppt bindsym j resize grow height 10 px or 5 ppt bindsym Return mode "default" bindsym Escape mode "default" } Note: the scratchpad and the for_window above together are the honest template for every such desk toy: a quake terminal, a music player, a chat pane. Resize once and the numbers persist; no xdotool scripts needed, and it keeps its size on any monitor. 12 Hero vocabulary The commands and one-liners that finish the road: Spell What it does i3-msg 'workspace 3' Drive the WM from a shell or script (same grammar as bindsyms). i3-msg restart Restart without losing your session, from a terminal. i3-msg 'layout tabbed' Change layout of current workspace remotely. i3-nagbar -m "text" -B "btn" action That yellow warning bar; very useful in your own confirm dialogs. i3-config-wizard The declawed starter generator — rerun freely to inspect sane defaults. i3-diag Collect all runtime info for bug reports (also fine for “why is my bar empty”). i3-msg exec xterm Start apps through the WM, following startup-id focus rules. i3-dump-log What went wrong, in order of when it did. xev Find keysym/code numbers for binds. i3-config-validator Lint the config before reload rejects it. And the man pages that finish a hero: i3 (the user guide lives here), i3status , and i3's online user guide if your man page is minimal (or if you run the Wayland twin, the same guide is almost fully applicable under sway ). Note: and the meta-skill of the whole page: i3 rewards dictating the exact one line that fixes today's annoyance, then stopping. A 120-line config you can hold in your head beats a 1200-line config you barely survive. 13 Your desk, day by day Progress below is stored in this browser ( localStorage ) only. 0 / 12 RESET i3 installed; startx lands in the config wizard, and you chose Super on purpose Config lives in ~/.config/i3/config , is under version control, and $mod+Shift+c reload works Navigated a full day with only $mod + letters, no wallpaper-peeking mouse r
iDontBelieve: This is probably some Internal Error from Cloudflare 195.770 Unique Visitors in the Last Month? Cloudflare is trying to give me a FALSE sensation of the number of visits. I don't believe on this results Cloudflare developers, please fix this problem... If the results point to 10 vistors in one single month I would believe. Why the number cannot be right A unique visitor is a decision, not a fact. The dashboard has to guess whether two requests are the same person, and it guesses with an address, a user agent, a cookie or a fingerprint. When the address changes, the guess becomes a new person. Every scanner that rotates through a pool of proxies is counted as a crowd. This site is a few static pages with no forms and no reason to be linked from anywhere. A hundred and ninety five thousand unique visitors would mean that one in every few thousand people on the planet found it in a month, and that none of them left a comment anywhere. That is not statistics, that is an artefact. The uncomfortable possibility There is another reading, and it is worse than a bug: the number is correct, and almost all of it is automated traffic. If the bots are the majority, then the dashboard is not inflating anything, it is showing exactly what the Internet is made of. A site with no audience and no promotion would then be receiving hundreds of thousands of requests from scripts that have no idea what they are reading. I prefer the bug. It is easier to fix and much less sad. What I trust I trust the log lines I can read, the requests I can group by hand, and the slow accumulation of visits that come back on the same day of the week. Those numbers are small and boring, and they are the only ones that describe a reader. So, Cloudflare developers, please fix this problem. If the results point to 10 visitors in one single month, I would believe.

ifPoem: Logic Without Math or Numbers If(true) { It is what I can see { While if { you keep your head when others lose theirs and blame the weather of your face, and while if you can trust yourself when every clock in the room disagrees with your pulse, you will still have to walk into the morning as if the morning were a door that opens only for the one who does not kick it. While if you wait and not be tired by waiting, the waiting itself becomes a kind of work, and work, when it is honest, is a kind of waiting that does not ask to be praised. While if { you can dream and not make dreams your master, you will learn that a dream is a lamp and not a house, and while if you can think and not make thoughts your aim, you will find that thought is a tool and not a throne. While if you meet with Triumph and Disaster and treat those two impostors just the same, you will still feel the heat of both, because the body does not take advice from poems, and the heart does not read footnotes. While if you can bear to hear the truth you spoke twisted by knaves to make a trap for fools, you will also bear the quieter trap of silence, which is how a room teaches a person to vanish without leaving. While if { you watch the things you gave your life to broken, and stoop and build them up with worn-out tools, you will discover that the tools were never the point, and the stooping was. While if you make a heap of all your winnings and risk it on one turn of pitch-and-toss, and lose, and start again at your beginnings, and never breathe a word about your loss, the loss will still speak in the way you hold a cup, in the way you count the days, in the way you flinch at luck as if luck were a dog that once bit you and now sits politely at the door. While if { you can force your heart and nerve and sinew to serve their turn long after they are gone, and so hold on when there is nothing in you except the Will which says to them: Hold on, you will learn that will is not a shout but a habit, and habit is not a prison if you chose the bars. While if you talk with crowds and keep your virtue, virtue will still be a word until it costs you something you wanted to keep. While if you walk with kings and not lose the common touch, the common touch will still require you to remember the names of people who will never walk with kings, and to remember them without making a theater of remembering. While if { neither foes nor loving friends can hurt you, someone will still hurt you, because love is a kind of accuracy and accuracy finds the place that bruises. While if all men count with you, but none too much, you will still wake at night counting one more than you meant to, and that one will be the measure of your remaining humanity. While if you can fill the unforgiving minute with sixty seconds’ worth of distance run, the minute will still be unforgiving, and the distance will still be yours, and the running will still be a way of saying you have not yet agreed to stop. While if { rain falls on the roof you built with care, the rain is not a verdict, only water doing what water does. While if drought comes after you have planted as if the ground were a promise, the ground was never a promise, only soil, and soil keeps its own counsel. While if a river changes course in the night, the maps you loved become a kind of fiction, and while if you redraw them without cursing the river, you will have practiced a citizenship older than nations. While if the wind takes the seed you meant for spring, some other field may green because of your loss, and you may never see it, and that unseen greening is still a kind of justice the world performs without witnesses. While if { a child asks you a question you cannot answer, the honest answer is the shape of the question held open. While if you answer too quickly, you close a door that was trying to become a window. While if you teach by fear, the lesson will last until the fear is gone, and then the lesson will go with it. While if you teach by example, the example will outlive your explanations, which is both a comfort and a warning. While if you forget a birthday, a name, a small kindness you once received, the forgetting does not erase the debt; it only hides the ledger until grief or gratitude finds it again. While if { work is only money, the days will thin until they are transparent and you can see through them to nothing. While if work is only pride, the pride will crack at the first public failure, and the crack will let in a weather you cannot budget for. While if you labor for a thing you cannot name, you may still be feeding a hunger that has no mouth. While if you labor for a neighbor, the labor becomes a language, and languages, even clumsy ones, keep people from becoming strangers in the same kitchen. While if you refuse the easy lie at the meeting, the room may cool around you, and while if you tell the easy lie, the room may warm, and you will carry the temperature home in your throat. While if { love arrives like weather, you cannot vote it out of office. While if love leaves like weather, you cannot sue the sky. While if you try to own a person the way a lock owns a key, you will find that people are not keys, and locks rust from the inside. While if you stay when staying is a vow and not a habit, staying becomes a craft. While if you go when going is mercy and not escape, going becomes a kind of remaining elsewhere. While if jealousy speaks first, it will speak in the voice of a child who thinks love is a ration. While if patience speaks first, it will still have to speak again, because patience is not a single sentence. While if { the body fails in small ways first, the small ways are rehearsals. While if you take every cry into your chest, your chest will become a warehouse, and warehouses are not hearts. Introdução: A Necessidade de Mudança de Abordagem Contexto Operacional As forças de segurança e militares ao redor do mundo enfrentam um desafio crescente: a necessidade de intervir em situações complexas sem recorrer à força letal desnecessária. Tradicionalmente, a abordagem baseada puramente em táticas militares ou policiais convencionais tem resultadod em elevadas taxas de casualties entre civis, erosão da confiança das comunidades e, em muitos casos, consolidação do poder dos grupos criminosos que se fintem operadores legítimos. 1.1 A Falha dos Modelos Tradicionais O modelo tradicional de "identificar, perseguir, neutralizar" esbarra em limitações crucuais: Falha na Distinção: Não consegue diferenciar entre combatentes reais, cúmplices menores e civis envolvidos por circunstância; Erosão da Legitimidade: Quando a população sente que é alvo de operações militarizadas, coopera menos com as forças de segurança; Radicalização Secundária: Operadores desnecessários podem criar mais reclutas do que neutralizam; Questões Jurídicas: Ações desproporcionais violam o Direito Internacional Humanitário e convenções de direitos humanos. Alerta Operacional Desempenhar ações com a mesma lógica que os grupos criminosos — mesmo que com intenções distintas — não apenas é antiético como compromete a legitimidade institucional. Crime é Crime, independentemente de quem o comete. 2. Diferenciação: Inocentes vs. Culpados Este é o conceito fundamental que separa operações eficazes das que perpetuam violência cíclica. Não existe "colateral" quando se falha na diferenciação. 2.1 Arquitetura de Participação Todo grupo criminoso ou de perturbação possui uma estrutura hierárquica que pode ser mapeada: 👑 Nível 1: Líderes Estratégicos Tomam decisões de longo prazo, organizam logistics, estabelecem agendas políticas ou criminais. Este grupo é o principal alvo para desmantelamento. 🎯 Nível 2: Executores Diretos Realizam ações específicas sob ordens. Podem ser persuadidos a deserir ou cooperar com informações sobre os líderes. 🛡️ Nível 3: Cúmplices por Circunstância Fornecedores locais, informadores não conscientes, comunidade que tolera por medo ou necesidade económica. 🌱 Nível 4: Potenciais Recrutas Jovens ou marginalizados susceptíveis a serem recrutados. Intervenção precoce aqui previne expansão do grupo. 2.2 Indicadores de Distinção Matriz de Análise de Participação Indicador Participação Ativa Participação Passiva Nenhuma Participação Conhecimento Operacional Conhece planos, locais, rotas Sabe que algo ocorre, mas não detalhes Ignora totalmente Contribuição Económica Financia, fornece recursos diretamente Compra produtos de forma incidental Não interage com economia do grupo Apoio Logístico Hospeda, transporta intencionalmente Não oferece resistência, mas não ajuda Coopera com autoridades Motivação Ideologia, ganância, vingança ativa Medo, necessidade económica Neutralidade ou oposição Princípio Operacional Antes de qualquer intervenção, a questão fundamental deve ser: "Esta pessoa é essencial para a estrutura do grupo, ou é um elo que pode ser substituído sem comprometer as operações?" Se a resposta for "não essencial", o foco deve ser desengajamento, não eliminação. 3. Habilidades Psicológicas e Sociais para Análise Superior A capacidade de compreender comportamentos, motivos e estruturas sociais é tão crítica quanto qualquer tática de intervenção física. 3.1 Inteligência Social Operacional Desenvolver inteligência social não significa fingir ser amigo — significa compreender as dinâmicas reais das comunidades e grupos: Competências Essenciais Mapeamento de Redes Sociais: Identificar quem influencia quem, não apenas quem é o "chefe" aparente; Análise de Narrativas Locais: Compreender quais histórias, mitos e justificativas sustentam o grupo; Linguagem e Cultura: Falar a língua, compreender tabus e normas locais; Empatia Analítica: Entender por que alguém se juntou ao grupo sem racionalizar ou justificar a conduta; Detecção de Incongruências: Notar quando alguém age de forma inconsistente com seu papel declarado. 3.2 Técnicas de Persuasão e Desengajamento Muitas vezes, é possível desfazerrecrutar ou retirar suporte sem esforço físico: Oferta de Alternativas: Fornecer caminhos legítimos para quem participou por necessidade económica; Proteção ao Desengajar: Garantir segurança a quem decide cooperar ou abandonar o grupo; Quebra de Narrativa: Expôr contradições entre a retórica do grupo e sua realidade; Apoio Psicossocial: Trabalhar com comunidades para reduzir o apelo das narrativas extremistas. 4. Infiltration sem Apresentação como Police ou Militar Nota Ética Infiltration deve sempre ser feita dentro do quadro legal e ético, com supervisão adequada e com objetivos definidos. Melhores Práticas Documente todas as fontes, métodos e raciocínios. Uma análise rastreável permite revisão, correção de erros e responsabilidade. Isso protege tanto os operadores quanto os cidadãos. 6. Exemplos Internacionais: Polícia e Military em Diferentes Países Para entender as diferenças de abordagem, examine como diferentes nações lidam com desafios de segurança: 6.1 Modelo Escandinavo (Suécia, Noruega, Dinamarca) Característica Abordagem Resultados Foco Prevenção, intervenção precoce, reintegração Baixas taxas de reincidência Uso da Força Último recurso, mínimo necessário Poucos feridos em operações civis Relação Comunitária Alta confiança, cooperação ativa Informação flui naturalmente Estrutura Polícia civilizada, mínimo militareização Percepção de legitimidade alta 6.2 Modelo de Segurança Comunitária (Colômbia pós-conflito) A Colômbia desenvolveu abordagens significativas para lidar com grupos armados sem recorrer a táticas puramente militarizadas: Guardianes de Comunidad: Membros da comunidade treinados para proteger suas próprias áreas sem constituir grupo armado; Justiça Restaurativa: Foco em reparação de danos em vez de apenas punição; Programas de Desmovilização: Oferecer alternativas reais para combatentes que desejam sair da luta. 6.3 Modelos de Militaryização Extrema Países que adotaram militarização completa da polícia frequentemente enfrentam: Escalada de Violência: Táticas letais levam a retalições; Perda de Inteligência: A comunidade para de cooperar; Custo Humano: Ferimentos e mortes entre civis não combatentes; Questões Jurídicas Internacionais: Violações do Direito Internacional podem levar a sanções e tribunais. Leitura Crítica O sucesso de diferentes modelos varia conforme o contexto histórico, cultural e político de cada nação. O que funciona em um ambiente pode falhar em outro. Both organizations attempt to manage peace, security, and cooperation across nations, but they do so through radically different mechanisms. Understanding how they work — down to the procedural and structural level — reveals both their strengths and their systemic limitations. Submit Answer 2 §2 — NATO: Structure, Decision-Making & Operations Level 2: Technical 2.1 What NATO Is (and Is Not) NATO — the North Atlantic Treaty Organization — is a treaty-based political and military alliance founded in 1949 by the North Atlantic Treaty (also called the Washington Treaty). It currently has 32 member countries (as of 2024, with Sweden the most recent accession). Critical technical fact: NATO does not own a standing army. It does not maintain its own troops, ships, or aircraft as a permanent force. Instead, member countries provide forces and equipment when they agree to missions. NATO's role is to make nationally-owned forces and systems operate together — this is called interoperability . 2.2 Organizational Structure NATO's organization has political and military dimensions: Political Structure North Atlantic Council (NAC) — the principal political decision-making body. Every member country is represented. It can meet at ambassador, ministerial, or heads-of-state level. The Secretary General chairs the Council and facilitates consultation and coordination but does not decide policy on behalf of members. Secretary General — the chief civilian official, currently Jens Stoltenberg (as of 2024). Provides continuity, chairs meetings, and represents NATO externally. Military Structure Military Committee (MC) — composed of member countries' senior military representatives. Advises the NAC on military matters. International Military Staff (IMS) — supports the Military Committee. Allied Command Operations (ACO) — plans and conducts all NATO operations. Headed by the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), a US four-star general who also commands US European Command. Allied Command Transformation (ACT) — leads work on adapting military forces, capabilities, and doctrine for future challenges. This separation between political decision-making (NAC) and military command (ACO/ACT) is fundamental: politicians decide what to do; military structures plan and execute how to do it . 2.3 Decision-Making: Consensus The most important technical detail about NATO is its decision rule. NATO decides by consensus, not by majority vote. Members discuss proposals until none objects. In practice, "silence" can signal agreement in some procedural contexts. A single member can therefore prevent the Alliance from adopting a decision. This applies across the entire committee system, not just at the top political level. Consensus means unanimity in effect . Every member has a veto. This is a deliberate design choice that protects sovereignty but can slow decision-making significantly. 2.4 Article 5: Collective Defense Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty states: "The Parties agree that an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all and consequently they each, in exercise of the right of individual or collective self-defence recognised by Article 51 of the Charter of the United Nations, will assist the Party or Parties so attacked..." Key technical clarifications: Article 5 is a commitment to assist , not a requirement that every member take the same military action. Each Ally takes the action it deems necessary — which may include armed force, but could also include logistical support, intelligence sharing, or other forms of assistance. The commitment operates within the framework of the UN Charter (Article 51 recognizes the inherent right of self-defense). Historical fact: NATO has invoked Article 5 exactly once : after the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States. This single invocation demonstrates that collective defense can involve varied forms of assistance — not only combat deployments. Member countries contributed in different ways: some deployed troops to Afghanistan, others provided logistical support, intelligence, or overflight permissions. 2.5 Funding Model NATO's funding has two broad channels: Channel Description Example National defense spending Members pay for their own forces, equipment, and most costs of deploying them. This is the larger, indirect contribution to Alliance capability. Each country maintains its own military budget; the 2% of GDP guideline is a spending target, not a NATO fee. Common funding Members make direct contributions to shared budgets. NATO identifies three principal common-funded areas: civil budget (administerial costs), military budget (command structure), and the NATO Security Investment Programme (NSIP) for shared infrastructure and capabilities. Costs of maintaining NATO headquarters, command facilities, and jointly-owned infrastructure are shared. A NATO decision to launch a non-Article 5 operation does not oblige every ally to contribute troops. Members choose whether and how to contribute. Generally, countries cover the costs of their own deployments; shared budgets cover agreed common costs. Article 5 operations are treated somewhat differently in terms of expectations. 2.6 Interoperability & Standardization Since NATO has no standing army, its technical core is making national forces work together. This requires: Communications interoperability — forces must be able to communicate across national boundaries using compatible systems. Shared doctrine and procedures — common operating procedures (e.g., NATO Standardization Agreements, STANAGs) ensure units from different countries can coordinate. Shared infrastructure — bases, airfields, ports, and logistics hubs that multiple nations can use. Common equipment standards — particularly important for munitions, fuel, and logistical supplies. Real limitation: Interoperability problems have occurred in operations. For example, during early Afghan operations, coalition partners sometimes struggled with incompatible radios, differing rules of engagement, and varying logistics systems. These are not abstract concerns — they directly affect mission effectiveness. 2.7 Real NATO Operations KFOR — Kosovo Force (1999–present) Deployed on 12 June 1999, following a 78-day NATO air campaign (Operation Allied Force) against Serbian forces in Kosovo. KFOR's role includes maintaining a safe and secure environment. NATO continues to describe its presence as an active mission — currently around 4,000 troops from 30+ nations. Real example: KFOR is a non-Article 5 mission. It was not triggered by an armed attack on a NATO member. It demonstrates that NATO can conduct operations under specific mandates with participating coalitions, without invoking collective defense. ISAF — International Security Assistance Force, Afghanistan (2003–2014) NATO took the lead of ISAF in August 2003, its first operational role outside Europe. At its height (circa 2010–2011), ISAF included more than 130,000 personnel from NATO and partner countries. The mission ended in December 2014, transitioning to the smaller Resolute Support mission. Bad decision: The mission's scope expanded well beyond initial goals, and the exit strategy was poorly defined. Multiple NATO allies made decisions that proved unsound in hindsight — including underestimation of the insurgency's resilience and overestimation of the Afghan government's capacity. These were not failures of any single country; they were collective errors in judgment across the Alliance. 2.8 NATO's Strengths & Weaknesses (Balanced Assessment) Strengths Weaknesses Deterrence through collective defense commitment Consensus rule can paralyze decision-making when members disagree Interoperability standards enable multinational operations No standing army — dependence on national contributions Political cohesion among democratic members Burden-sharing disputes (2% GDP target not universally met) Article 5 invoked only once — shows restraint, not automatic escalation Expansion debates create geopolitical friction (e.g., Russia relations) Balanced criticism: NATO members have made bad decisions — including the 2003 Iraq War divergence (some members supported, others opposed, causing internal strain), the Libya intervention's post-conflict planning gap (2011), and Afghanistan's exit strategy failure. These errors are not unique to any one country or administration. Every major NATO member contributed to some form of poor judgment at some point. 3 §3 — ONU (United Nations): Structure & Mechanics Level 3: Advanced 3.1 What the UN Is The United Nations (UN, or ONU in Romance languages) is a global international organization founded in 1945 after World War II. It currently has 193 member states. Unlike NATO, the UN has a much broader mandate encompassing peace and security, human rights, development, humanitarian aid, and international law. Critical technical fact: The UN does not have its own army. Member states volunteer military and police personnel for peacekeeping missions. The UN reimburses countries for personnel and equipment under established arrangements. Peacekeeping forces are contributed by member states, not employed by the UN as a permanent force. 3.2 The Six Principal Organs The UN Charter establishes six principal organs: General Assembly (GA) — all 193 member states; main deliberative body. Security Council (SC) — 15 members; primary responsibility for international peace and security. Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) — coordinates economic and social work. Trusteeship Council — suspended regular operations in 1994 after the last trust territory gained independence. Still exists in form. International Court of Justice (ICJ) — the principal judicial organ; settles disputes between states. Secretariat — headed by the Secretary-General; carries out day-to-day work. 3.3 Security Council: Structure & Veto Power The Security Council has 15 members: 5 permanent members (P5): China, France, Russia, United Kingdom, United States. 10 non-permanent members: elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms. For substantive decisions (peace and security, sanctions, authorization of force): At least 9 votes are required, including the concurrence of all five permanent members. A negative vote by any P5 member blocks adoption — this is the veto . An abstention by a permanent member is not a veto; a resolution can pass with 9 affirmative votes even if a P5 member abstains. For procedural matters : 9 affirmative votes, without the permanent-member concurrence rule. Real examples of vetoes: Russia has vetoed resolutions on Syria multiple times (e.g., 2011–2020 period), blocking UN action on the Syrian civil war. The United States has vetoed resolutions critical of Israel, including multiple resolutions on Gaza and Palestinian statehood. China has vetoed resolutions on human rights issues and on sanctions against certain countries. France and the UK have used vetoes historically (e.g., on decolonization issues in the 1950s–60s); the UK last used its veto in 1989. The veto system means that any one of the five most powerful states can block UN action on matters of peace and security . This is a structural feature that reflects the post-WWII power distribution — it is simultaneously a guarantee against UN action against great powers and a guarantee that the UN often cannot act when a great power opposes action. 3.4 General Assembly: Functions & Limits The General Assembly includes all 193 member states, each with one vote . Its functions include: Deliberation and recommendation on international issues (broad mandate). Electing non-permanent Security Council members. Appointing the Secretary-General (on Security Council recommendation). Approving the UN regular budget and assessing member contributions. Admitting new members. Voting rules: Important questions (peace and security recommendations, budgetary matters, admission of new members, election of SC members): require a two-thirds majority . Other questions : simple majority. Many resolutions are adopted by consensus (no recorded vote) after negotiation. Crucially, General Assembly resolutions are generally not binding on states (unlike Security Council decisions under Article 25, which member states agree to accept and carry out). The GA's authority to approve the budget and assess contributions is a major exception — member states are obligated to pay their assessed share. 3.5 UN Peacekeeping: Principles & Mandates The Security Council decides whether to establish, maintain, or expand peacekeeping operations and sets their mandates. UN peacekeeping is guided by three core principles : Consent of the main parties — peacekeeping requires consent from the host country and major parties to the conflict. Impartiality — peacekeepers do not take sides, though they are not neutral in the face of peace agreement violations. Non-use of force except in self-defense and defense of the mandate — peacekeeping is not peace enforcement. Robust mandates can authorize force at the tactical level in specified circumstances, but peacekeeping remains distinct from combat operations aimed at imposing a solution. Important distinction: Peacekeeping ≠ peace enforcement. When a peacekeeping mission is deployed where consent has broken down, or when it is given a robust mandate to use offensive force, it moves toward peace enforcement — and this creates practical and legal challenges. The distinction matters technically and operationally. 3.6 Real UN Peacekeeping Missions UNIFIL — United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (1978–present) Established in 1978 to confirm Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon, restore peace, and help the Lebanese government restore authority. After the 2006 Lebanon War, the Security Council expanded UNIFIL's mandate: monitoring the cessation of hostilities, supporting the Lebanese armed forces in the south, and facilitating humanitarian access. UNIFIL currently has around 10,000 personnel from 45+ contingents. It operates along the Blue Line (the demarcation between Israel and Lebanon). Real example: UNIFIL illustrates peacekeeping with a limited mandate in a complex environment. Its effectiveness is constrained by the consent of host parties — when Hezbollah or Israel operate in the area, UNIFIL's ability to act depends on political agreements it does not control. UNMISS — United Nations Mission in South Sudan (2011–present) Established in 2011 after South Sudan's independence. After violence erupted in December 2013, the Security Council refocused the mission on civilian protection, human rights monitoring, and support for humanitarian assistance. The mission has a large protection of civilians component, with "protection sites" where civilians seek shelter. Bad decision: The international community — including UN Security Council members — failed to anticipate the scale of the 2013 violence and was slow to reinforce the mission. All parties to the conflict bear responsibility for the violence. The UN's slow response reflects systemic problems in peacekeeping escalation, not any single member's failure. MONUSCO — United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (2010–present) Began in 2010, succeeding an earlier UN mission (MONUC). Its mandate includes civilian protection, support for stabilization and peace consolidation, and protection of humanitarian personnel. MONUSCO has a Force Intervention Brigade — a unique feature that authorizes offensive operations to neutralize armed groups, going beyond traditional peacekeeping. Innovation: The Force Intervention Brigade (2013) represents an attempt to adapt peacekeeping to situations where consent is imperfect and armed groups threaten civilians directly. It is controversial because it blurs the line between peacekeeping and peace enforcement. 3.7 UN Funding The UN is financed through: Assessed contributions — member states are assigned contribution rates based on capacity to pay (GDP, debt burden, etc.). The General Assembly approves the budget and sets the scale. Voluntary contributions — for specific programs (UNICEF, WFP, UNHCR, etc.). For peacekeeping operations, a separate assessment scale applies. All member states are legally obligated to pay their assessed share. The five permanent Security Council members pay a larger share because of their special responsibility for international peace and security (the P5 have higher assessment ceilings).
