Master sources (check every step): Handbook:AMD64, Full/Installation, Media/Disks/Stage/Base/Kernel/Bootloader, Portage Profiles, Wiki KDE/GNOME/PipeWire/Nftables/OpenSSH/WireGuard/SELinux/AppArmor/Hardened, man emerge/make.conf/fstab/cryptsetup. Research verified 2025-2026 Handbook flow. 0 — Introduction: What Gentoo Is (And Is Not) Welcome, new friend. If you know nothing about Gentoo , start here. Gentoo is a source-based Linux distribution. Most distributions give you prebuilt binaries. Gentoo gives you recipes called ebuilds and a package manager called Portage with its famous command emerge . You compile software for your machine with your flags. Result: total control, total learning, total responsibility. This means install takes hours, sometimes days. Tip: this is normal. Gentoo is a teacher that charges tuition in compile time. You will choose init system ( OpenRC default classic, or systemd ), USE flags (global options like -gnome -kde pulseaudio ), profile , kernel type, bootloader, filesystem. Nothing hidden. Who should install Gentoo ? Curious people who want to understand Linux from disk label to desktop pixel. Who should not? Anyone needing a 20 -minute install before a meeting. Tip: keep a second computer or phone nearby for docs and coffee. Official sources you will use constantly: Handbook:AMD64 overview, Full Installation guide, Gentoo Wiki , forums.gentoo.org , packages.gentoo.org , bugs.gentoo.org . Bookmark them now. Tip: never follow random blog commands blindly; always cross-check the Handbook version for your arch. Versions in this guide: arch amd64 , UEFI + GPT assumed, OpenRC default with systemd notes. What you need: 64 -bit PC, 4 GB RAM minimum ( 8 GB+ happy), 40 GB disk minimum ( 100 GB+ for desktop + sources), wired net preferred, 8 GB USB stick, backup of all data. Tip: wired Ethernet saves hours of Wi-Fi firmware pain on first install. Time: 1 evening for base, 1-2 days for desktop + kernel + hardening. Security mindset from zero: we will verify downloads, encrypt where sensible, harden kernel, use SELinux or AppArmor options, firewall with nftables , least privilege, updates. Tip: security is a process, not a package. Every step below has a security note. 1 — Boot Media, Networking, Disks Step 1 : get media from gentoo.org/downloads/amd64 . Two flavors: Minimal Installation CD (small, text only) and LiveGUI (graphical). Tip: newbies take LiveGUI for comfort, Minimal for focus. Both boot same Handbook path. Verify checksum/signature per Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Media . Write with balenaEtcher , Rufus , Ventoy , or dd . Example: dd if= install-amd64-minimal.iso of= /dev/sdX bs= 4M status=progress. Tip: triple-check /dev/sdX with lsblk or you wipe the wrong disk. Boot in UEFI mode if target is UEFI. Connect net: NetworkManager on LiveGUI, or net-setup / ip + wpa_supplicant on Minimal. Test with ping 8.8.8.8 and ping gentoo.org . Tip: if Wi-Fi needs firmware, plug cable now; fight Wi-Fi after install. Set sshd password if you want remote help, and set clock with chrony / ntpd . Step 2 — disks: see Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Disks . Use lsblk , fdisk -l , gdisk or parted . We assume UEFI + GPT. Layout: 1 GiB EFI System Partition FAT32, swap (match RAM if hibernate, else 4-8 GB ), rest for root ext4 or btrfs or xfs + optional /home . Tip: separate /home saves future reinstall pain. LUKS-encrypt root/home now if laptop — see Security chapter. Example with parted : mklabel gpt, mkpart ESP fat32 1MiB 1025MiB , set 1 esp on, mkpart swap 1025MiB 9GiB , mkpart root 9GiB 100% . Format: mkfs.fat -F32 /dev/nvme0n1p1 , mkswap + swapon , mkfs.ext4 or mkfs.btrfs -L gentoo . Mount root at /mnt/gentoo , mkdir /mnt/gentoo/efi and mount ESP there (Handbook UEFI path) or /boot for BIOS layout. Tip: mount ESP at /efi for systemd-boot/dist-kernel style, at /boot/efi only if you know why. Sources: Handbook Media, Handbook Disks, Arch Wiki EFI/GPT pages for background, Gentoo Wiki LUKS articles. Tip: photograph partition table with phone before formatting — future you says thanks. 2 — Stage3, Chroot, Portage Basics Step 3 — stage: a stage 3 is your seed system, separate from ISO. Pick at gentoo.org/downloads/amd64 matching init: stage3-amd64-openrc or stage3-amd64-systemd , multilib default, desktop flavor if graphical (name contains desktop). See Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Stage . Tip: desktop stage saves hours of USE-flag wrestling for GNOME/KDE. Download + .DIGESTS + .asc, verify with sha512sum and gpg . Unpack with tar xpvf stage3-*.tar.xz --xattrs-include='*.*' --numeric-owner inside /mnt/gentoo . Tip: --numeric-owner and xattrs are not optional; skipping breaks permissions. Step 4 — chroot: copy DNS: cp --dereference /etc/resolv.conf /mnt/gentoo/etc/ . Mount proc sys dev run or use arch-chroot /mnt/gentoo helper. For UEFI mount ESP at /efi before chroot. See Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Base . Inside: emerge-webrsync to fetch Portage tree snapshot, then optional emerge --sync . Read news with eselect news read . Tip: always read news before first big emerge; it warns about profile/migration breakage. Select profile: eselect profile list , eselect profile set N . Example desktop plasma or gnome , with systemd variant if needed. Check with eselect profile show . Configure make.conf : COMMON_FLAGS= -O2 -march=native -pipe , MAKEOPTS= -jN+1 where N =cores, USE flags, VIDEO_CARDS, INPUT_DEVICES, ACCEPT_LICENSE. Tip: -march=native is fast but binaries not portable; use generic x86-64 if you clone disks. Set eselect repository , mirrors with mirrorselect . Configure system files: /etc/fstab (use UUIDs from blkid ), hostname in /etc/conf.d/hostname ( OpenRC ) or /etc/hostname ( systemd ), timezone via eselect timezone / symlink /etc/localtime , locale in /etc/locale.gen + locale-gen + eselect locale , keymap, root password with passwd , networking ( NetworkManager easiest for desktop, dhcpcd / netifrc for servers). Tip: UUID in fstab prevents boot fail after disk reorder. Sources: Handbook Stage, Handbook Base, Wiki: Portage/Profiles , Wiki: MAKEOPTS , man make.conf , man emerge . Tip: keep a text log of every command; Gentoo forums love logs when helping. 3 — Kernel: Distribution vs Manual Compile See Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Kernel . Three roads: sys-kernel/gentoo-kernel-bin (prebuilt, fastest, great for newbies), sys-kernel/gentoo-kernel (source-built distro kernel, auto updates, needs installkernel + initramfs), sys-kernel/gentoo-sources (fully manual, you configure/compile). Tip: start with -bin to get to desktop today, switch to manual later for learning. Distro kernel path: emerge --ask sys-kernel/gentoo-kernel-bin sys-kernel/installkernel sys-kernel/dracut sys-firmware/linux-firmware sof-firmware sys-firmware/intel-microcode amd-ucode . Dracut builds initramfs for LUKS/LVM/btrfs. Check /efi or /boot for vmlinuz-6.x + initramfs . Tip: install linux-firmware + microcode before first boot or Wi-Fi/GPU may vanish. Enable installkernel USE for grub or systemd-boot layout. Manual path: emerge --ask sys-kernel/gentoo-sources sys-apps/pciutils usbutils , cd /usr/src/linux , make menuconfig (needs ncurses ). Essentials: 64 -bit, EFI stub, NVMe, SATA AHCI, ext4/btrfs built-in not module if root, drm amdgpu/i915/nouveau , sound, USB, networking. Tip: run lspci -k and lsmod on LiveGUI, photo it, enable exactly that hardware first. Build: make -j$(nproc) , make modules_install install . Takes 20 min to 2 hours by CPU. Keep .config backup in /root/kernel-config-YYYY-MM-DD . Initramfs when needed (LUKS/LVM/btrfs/UEFI): dracut --hostonly --kver 6.x.y-gentoo or genkernel --install initramfs . Verify ls -lh /boot /efi . Tip: if root is LUKS, test cryptsetup open before reboot or you lock yourself out. Sources: Handbook Kernel, Wiki: Kernel/Gentoo Kernel Upgrade Guide , Wiki: Dracut , Wiki: Genkernel , kernel.org docs. Tip: keep one known-good kernel + one new; never delete all old kernels. 4 — Bootloader, First Reboot, Post-Install Base See Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Bootloader . Default sys-boot/grub handles BIOS+UEFI. UEFI alt sys-boot/systemd-boot (simple, fast). Install: emerge --ask sys-boot/grub efibootmgr os-prober (skip os-prober if single boot). grub-install --target=x86_64-efi --efi-directory=/efi --bootloader-id=Gentoo , then grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg . Tip: --efi-directory must match where you mounted ESP (/efi vs /boot); mismatch = unbootable. For systemd-boot : bootctl install --esp-path=/efi , loader entries in /efi/loader/entries/gentoo.conf pointing to vmlinuz + initramfs + root UUID + rw . Tip: systemd-boot needs manual entry update per kernel unless installkernel hooks do it — check after each upgrade. Exit chroot, unmount: exit , umount -l /mnt/gentoo/dev{/shm,/pts,} , umount -R /mnt/gentoo , reboot , remove USB. First boot: login root, check dmesg | grep -i -E 'error|firmware|fail' , ip a , ping . Add user: useradd -m -G wheel,audio,video,usb,portage -s /bin/bash alice , passwd alice , install sudo + visudo (uncomment wheel). Tip: never daily-drive as root; sudo + wheel from day one. Base update discipline: emerge --sync (or emaint sync -a ), emerge --ask --verbose --update --deep --newuse @world , emerge --depclean , revdep-rebuild , eclean-dist --deep . Tip: update weekly, read elog with eselect news + elogv; small frequent merges beat yearly breakage. Sources: Handbook Bootloader, Wiki: GRUB2 , Wiki: Systemd-boot , man sudoers . Tip: snapshot btrfs subvolume or Clonezilla image right after first good boot. 5 — Kernel Hardening, MAC, Toolchain Security Hardening is where Gentoo shines. Baseline: updated kernel ( 6.x stable, never ancient), least modules, Secure Boot with custom keys via sbctl or sbsigntools if threat model needs. Tip: enable Secure Boot only after normal boot works; debug one layer at a time. Kernel self-protection (manual or via gentoo-kernel + sysctl): enable STACKPROTECTOR_STRONG , STRICT_KERNEL_RWX , STRICT_MODULE_RWX , SLAB_FREELIST_HARDENED , SHUFFLE_PAGE_ALLOCATOR , RANDOMIZE_BASE (KASLR), HARDENED_USERCOPY , SECURITY_LOCKDOWN_LSM , PAGE_TABLE_ISOLATION , RETPOLINE / IBRS mitigations, DEBUG_WX to find WX, disable /dev/mem /dev/kmem , LDISC_AUTOLOAD off, USER_NS_UNPRIVILEGED restrict if not needing containers. Tip: copy hardened .config fragment to /root and diff after each make olddefconfig. See Wiki: Hardened Gentoo , gentoo-hardened overlay, KSPP checklists. Mandatory Access Control — pick one : SELinux (strongest, steepest; selinux-base-policy , relabel, setenforce 1 ) or AppArmor (easier, profiles via apparmor-utils , aa-enforce ) . Tip: newbies start with AppArmor + firewall; graduate to SELinux on second install. Add hardened malloc via sys-libs/mimalloc-hw or hardened_malloc overlay for browsers, firejail or bubblewrap sandbox for Firefox . Toolchain: gcc with -fstack-protector-strong -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 -Wl,-z,RelRO,-z,Now -fPIE -pie via CFLAGS / LDFLAGS or hardened profile ( eselect profile hardened). Enable PIE + RELRO + NOW + SSP , verify with hardening-check / checksec . Tip: hardened flags can break exotic packages; keep per-package exceptions in /etc/portage/env, not global weaken. Boot/filesystem: LUKS2 ( cryptsetup ) with argon2id , detached header backup offline, fscrypt or eCryptfs only if needed, auditd rules for /etc/passwd /etc/shadow /boot , AIDE or samhain integrity DB on read-only USB. Tip: print LUKS recovery key on paper, store offsite; digital-only backup dies with disk. Sources: Gentoo Hardened project, Wiki: SELinux , Wiki: AppArmor , KSPP (kernel self-protection), man cryptsetup . Tip: change one hardening knob per reboot so you know what broke boot. 6 — Desktop: Plasma / GNOME, Graphics, Sound Pick profile first: eselect profile list | grep desktop , set default/linux/amd64/23.0/desktop/plasma or .../desktop/gnome (+ systemd variant if on systemd ). Set VIDEO_CARDS= amdgpu radeon intel nvidia as needed, INPUT_DEVICES= libinput synaptics . Tip: wrong VIDEO_CARDS = black screen; lspci | grep -i vga first. X or Wayland: xorg-server + xinit for classic, or Wayland via plasma-meta / gnome sessions. Install: emerge --ask kde-plasma/plasma-meta kde-apps/kdecore-meta sddm for KDE Plasma , or emerge --ask gnome-base/gnome gdm for GNOME . Lighter: i3 , sway , Xfce via xfce4-meta . Enable DM: rc-update add sddm default ( OpenRC ) or systemctl enable sddm ( systemd ). Tip: test with startx as user before enabling DM; DM hides errors. Firmware + microcode + graphics: linux-firmware amdgpu-ucode intel-microcode amd-ucode mesa vulkan-loader libva-vdpau-driver , kernel DRM built-in. Sound: pipewire wireplumber pipewire-pulse alsa-utils pavucontrol . Tip: PipeWire + WirePlumber is modern default; enable pipewire service per user. Fonts: noto , corefonts , fontconfig . Printing: cups . Bluetooth: bluez . Apps baseline: firefox (set USE=hardened pie ), thunderbird , libreoffice , vlc , gimp , keepassxc , flatpak optional for closed apps. Tip: Flatpak for Spotify/Discord/Steam keeps base clean; native emerge for everything else. Sources: Wiki: KDE , Wiki: GNOME , Wiki: Xorg , Wiki: PipeWire , eselect profile docs. Tip: emerge -pv before big desktop merge to see USE changes; veto surprises early. 7 — Network, Firewall, SSH, Updates, Backups Firewall default-deny with nftables (modern) or iptables legacy. Install nftables , enable, rules: allow lo , established, 22 only from LAN if needed, 80/443 out, drop rest, rate-limit SSH 3/min . Or use ufw / firewalld wrapper. Tip: test firewall over console first; lockout over SSH with no IPMI is a long walk. Add fail2ban for SSH, usbguard for BadUSB. SSH: openssh , PermitRootLogin no , PasswordAuthentication no (keys in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys 600 ), Port 2222 optional, AllowUsers alice . Tip: ssh-copy-id then disable passwords; one key leak beats thousand brute forces. VPN: wireguard-tools for road warriors. DNS: systemd-resolved or dnscrypt-proxy + DNSSEC. Updates + integrity: weekly emaint sync -a; emerge -uDN @world; emerge --depclean; revdep-rebuild; eclean-dist -d; updatedb; aide --check . Enable elogv / eselect news . Backups: borgbackup or restic to external LUKS disk + offsite, test restore quarterly. Tip: untested backup is rumor. Restore one file now to prove it works. Browser + user hardening: Firefox with uBlock Origin , NoScript or uMatrix , KeepassXC , separate profiles, bubblewrap / flatpak sandbox. Tip: Wayland + PipeWire + Flatpak Firefox is safest easy desktop sandbox. Sources: Wiki: Nftables , Wiki: OpenSSH , Wiki: WireGuard , Gentoo Security Handbook . Tip: run lynis audit or tiger check quarterly; fix reds first. 8 — Extra Security, Tips, Troubleshooting, Next Steps Extra: securelevel via sysctl kernel.kexec_load_disabled=1 kernel.dmesg_restrict=1 kernel.kptr_restrict=2 kernel.perf_event_paranoid=2 kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled=2 net.core.bpf_jit_harden=2 vm.mmap_rnd_bits=32 in /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf . sys-kernel/linux-firmware minimal (strip unused). Disable Bluetooth / Thunderbolt in BIOS if unused. Tip: sysctl + reboot + sysctl -a | grep setting to confirm; typos silently fail. Physical: BIOS password, boot order lock, LUKS + TPM2 + PIN via clevis optional, screen lock 5 min, usbguard block new devices when locked. Tip: encrypt swap or disable hibernate; cleartext swap leaks keys. Supply chain: verify ISOs, use gpg , app-portage/gemato , avoid random overlays; add eselect repository overlays sparingly. Troubleshooting: no boot? Check ESP mount, grub.cfg UUIDs, dracut --regenerate-all . Black screen? VIDEO_CARDS + firmware + eselect opengl . No net? dhcpcd vs NetworkManager conflict — pick one . Merge fail? Read build.log, emerge --info , search bugs.gentoo.org + forums with exact error. Tip: pastebin emerge --info + build log when asking help; helpers ignore vague 'it broke'. Next: join forums , IRC #gentoo , Reddit r/Gentoo , read GWN weekly news. Try distcc / ccache for speed, binpkg host for laptops. Tip: ccache size 10-20 GB cuts recompiles massively on desktop. Master source list: Handbook AMD64 + Full, Installation Media/Disks/Stage/Base/Kernel/Bootloader, Portage Profiles, KDE/GNOME/PipeWire/Nftables/OpenSSH/WireGuard/SELinux/AppArmor/Hardened Wiki pages, man pages for emerge make.conf fstab cryptsetup gpg sudoers sysctl . Tip: keep this HTML offline on USB; best rescue disk is docs you own. Gentoo installed? Harden weekly: emaint , emerge , eclean , aide , borgbackup . Tip: you now own your system — keep notes, keep backups, keep curiosity. Good luck from 0 to root.

knowledgeLabyrinth: Mind · Machine · Archive God(道) Descent Knowledge Labyrinth labyrinthus Not a maze to get lost in — a descent with the lights on. Twelve layers, from the instrument in your hand to the exit condition, every wall labelled and every claim carrying a receipt. MindOS, permission lattices, kernel diffs, regression, provenance — and the psychology of anyone, this author included, who mistakes a map for the ground. OdicforceSounds Monkey Blog Technical Edition Mixed With Reality Mind · Machine · Archive — always layered Layer 0 Threshold The Entry Is Already a Model Before the first wall, the instrument. Before you enter the labyrinth, notice the instrument you are using to enter it. A browser, a reader, a terminal, a mind — each is a model of the world with its own permission lattice, its own defaults, its own hidden assumptions about what can be seen and what can be done. The labyrinth does not begin where the first wall appears. It begins where the first model is applied. That is why the first layer is always the hardest to see: you are using it to look at everything else. ⌘ Model First ◈ See the Lens ◉ Reality Has Layers "A map is not the territory, but a bad map will make you walk off the edge and call it progress." Layer 1 Map Two Maps: Territory and Procedure The labyrinth is a place and a method. There are at least two things a labyrinth can mean. One is a territory : a space of possible states, paths, dead ends, and re-entries. Knowledge, risk, identity, law, power, code — each can be drawn as a topology and then walked. The other is a procedure : a set of moves, checks, proofs, tests, audits, decisions. The labyrinth here is not a place you are lost in; it is a sequence of constraints you satisfy or fail. Both maps are real. The error is to confuse which one you are holding. Confusion What it looks like Territory mistaken for procedure You think you are walking a real space, but you are only following rules that may not fit the ground. Procedure mistaken for territory You think you are obeying a method, but you are actually wandering without one and calling it exploration. Science without procedure You claim a fact while ignoring measurement, sampling, and falsifiability. Psychology without territory You name a feeling without checking what in the world actually triggers it. "The Monkey does not choose one map. The Monkey keeps both visible and switches deliberately." Layer 2 Kinds of Real What Kind of "Real" Are We Talking About? Not one stamp. Several lenses. "Real" is not a single stamp you can put on a thing and be done. There are at least these kinds, and they behave differently under pressure: Layer What it means Tag Nominal A thing with a name and a contract around the name. Label Observed A thing inferred from repeatable measurements. Science Regulatory A thing defined by rules, jurisdiction, and enforcement. Law Structural A thing whose role is defined by how it connects, not by what it is called. Graph Operational A thing that behaves a certain way when pressure is applied. Stress Provenancial A thing whose reality is tied to its line of descent, edits, receipts, and witnesses. Trace Psychological A thing real to the organism because it shapes perception, memory, fear, and action. Mind A labyrinth made of only one kind of "real" is usually a trap dressed as depth. The Monkey prefers multi-layered: name, measurement, rule, structure, behavior, provenance, and the felt reality of a nervous system — and a clear label on which layer you are currently debating. Layer 3 MindOS Architecture of a Mind-OS A working hypothesis with visible parts. A "MindOS" is a name for a working hypothesis: an internal system that coordinates perception, memory, action, inhibition, and revision. It is not necessarily a thing you can point to and hold; it is a thing you can point to by its effects and constraints. Useful descriptions of such a system usually include, at minimum: ◈ Input Filters ◉ State ⚙ Action Selection ⊡ Inhibition ↻ Revision ⌛ Provenance MindOS — working schema Input filters what gets admitted, ignored, or flagged for later State representation what is active, dormant, or evicted right now Action selection how one candidate behavior is chosen over another Inhibition what is suppressed, and by what authority Revision when and how the system updates its own model Provenance and memory what is kept, for how long, and in what form The interesting failures are rarely "the system is not smart enough." They are usually more specific: the filters were too narrow, the state was wrong, the inhibition was too strong or too weak, the revision was too late, or the provenance was missing when it mattered. "An operating system is not wise. It is consistent under pressure — or it is not." Layer 4 Activation Activation Maps Where activity concentrates, and why. If you look at a maze from enough distance, you do not see walls first. You see flow . In a nervous system, in a network, in a body of documents, in a political field, in a person's habits — there are regions where activity clusters, and regions where it is suppressed. Call them activation maps if you want a name. The name matters less than the observability. Activation maps are interesting because they reveal structure without needing a grand theory to explain it first: Where does attention repeatedly return? Where does it fail to return even when it should? Where does activity move quickly, and where does it stall? What suppresses it — internal rules, external force, fatigue, fear, design, reward? Do not confuse "active" with "true" and do not confuse "quiet" with "unimportant." Silence can be a dead end, but it can also be a bottleneck, a concealment, or a place where the wrong thing was removed from the map on purpose. "A quiet region is not always empty. Sometimes it is policed." Layer 5 Permissions Permissions and Borders A lattice, not a wall. Borders are often drawn as lines. A better model is a lattice: many points, many relations, and many possible paths between them, some allowed, some denied, some conditional. In a system with any seriousness, permissions are not one gate. They are a lattice of decisions: R Read W Write X Execute D Delegate N Deny A Audit V Revoke Permission If missing, what breaks Read You can act without seeing what you are acting on. Write The system can be steered by whoever can alter state. Execute Intent can remain inert if it cannot be run. Delegate Authority cannot scale without it, and bottlenecks grow. Deny Without explicit denial, exception becomes the rule. Audit Without audit, permission is only a claim. Revoke Without revocation, a lost edge can stay live for too long. "A wall is what you see. A lattice is what you must walk." Layer 6 BSD Lattice On the BSD Permission Lattice A small lattice, seriously studied. Unix file modes are a small but instructive example. They are not "ownership" in any grand sense; they are a lattice of execute, write, and read rights across three classes of actor — owner, group, other — plus a few metadata flags that change how the lattice behaves in practice. The form is compact. The lessons are not: Read, write, execute are not interchangeable abstractions. Each changes the character of access in a different way. Owner/group/other are a coarse social boundary. Coarse boundaries are cheap to think about and expensive to rely on when the world is finer than the model. Setuid/setgid/sticky are not decoration. They change the effective lattice by introducing transitions and constraints that can invert who is really in control at runtime. A permission model that is "mostly right" can still be attacked through the few places where the lattice is under-specified. Study it as a toy model of a deeper problem: access is not a single bit. It is a structure of transitions, and transitions are where surprises live. Permission lattice — coarse example Class r w x real meaning Owner read write exec the named owner Group read write exec membership edge Other read write exec everyone else Layer 7 Audit Audit and the Kernel Diff What can be checked when pressure is applied. A labyrinth is not just a structure. It is a structure plus the ability to detect when it has been altered. That is the role of audit. Without audit, "permission" is a claim. With audit, it becomes a traceable decision, or at least an attempt at one. A kernel diff is one kind of trace: a record that something changed, where, and under which conditions of authority. The hard part is not producing a diff. The hard part is making the diff meaningful when the thing being changed is itself the authority that decides what counts as a valid diff. That is why serious systems think in layers again: what changed who was able to change it what that change enables next who can see the change happened who can challenge it what can revert it what can prove it was or was not reverted If any one of those is missing, the labyrinth has a blind corridor. "A change with no receipt is a claim with no spine." Layer 8 Regression Regression and Provenance The maze must be able to remember. A labyrinth that cannot say what it was yesterday is not a labyrinth worth trusting. Regression is the warning that a later state may be worse in a way that is not obvious from the immediate change. Provenance is the record that lets you ask where a state came from, which choices led to it, and which constraints were in force at the time. These two ideas belong together because they fight different failures: Concern Question it asks Tag Regression did we lose something we previously had, even if the new thing looks better on one axis? Test Provenance can we reconstruct the path that led here, and does that record survive the next change? Receipt Psychological regression does the organism revert under stress to an older, narrower response? Stress Scientific regression does the later result still survive in a broader sample or a harder test? Replicate Without regression awareness, progress becomes a one-way ratchet that may be driving you into a corner. Without provenance, responsibility becomes a fog and accountability becomes a performance. Layer 9 Descent How Descent Actually Works Go down by choice, not by accident. A labyrinth can feel like descent if you wander into it. That is the cheap version. The technical version is different: descent is deliberate, and it is tracked. Real descent has properties: You know what layer you are on, at least approximately. You know what you are giving up to go deeper. You know what would count as coming back up. You leave a trace that is readable by the standards of the layer you left, not the layer you entered. You do not confuse depth with truth, nor novelty with insight. This is where the Monkey differs from the brute. The brute wants the deep thing because it is deep. The Monkey wants the deep thing because it is auditable , repeatable , and capable of failing in a way that teaches something . ↓ Deliberate ⌛ Tracked ↩ Reversible ◉ Real Layer 10 Exit The Exit Condition Exit is also a map. If you only think about entering, you will eventually be surprised by the exit problem: what does it mean to leave this labyrinth with something real? A good exit is not "I got out." A good exit is "I can show what I carried, what I changed, what I could not verify, and where the next blind corridor is." That is the difference between exploration and tourism. Tourism wants the story of having been there. Exploration wants the map, the receipt, and the next question. "If you descend without a trace, you did not descend. You disappeared." Layer 11 Monkey The Monkey's Way Hold the opposites, keep the trace. The Monkey does not prefer the territory to the procedure, or the procedure to the territory. The Monkey prefers to be able to name which one is being used at each step. That is the deeper technical discipline here: not "more depth," but better labelling of depth . MindOS, activation maps, permission lattice, audit, kernel diff, regression, provenance — these are not decorations. They are the tools that keep descent from becoming mystification. If you want the labyrinth to be real, do not make it prettier. Make it more checkable. Make it easier to enter and leave with something you can stand behind. Make it possible to tell, after the fact, whether the walls moved or only the walker did. That is the Monkey's technical ethic. Not clean. Not simple. But traceable. ◈ Checkable ◉ Mixed ⚙ Operational ⌛ Provenanced Traceable Descent Keep the Map, Keep the Receipt Descent is not a trick. It is a discipline: model, observe, constrain, audit, remember. If you lose the map, you are not exploring. If you lose the receipt, you are not learning. If you lose both, you are just moving. ← Back Top The Monkey O Macaco Path & Dream

learnHacking: How Hacking Happens — And How To Stop It Blue team to understand attack paths. Red team to break them. Lab only. No real targets without written permission. Ever. Ethics first — read or close this file: Only hack systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test (your lab, CTF, bug-bounty scope). Unauthorized access, credential cracking against real accounts, malware, ransomware, doxxing = crimes. This manual teaches concepts + defense + lab practice , not how to break into real systems. If in doubt, defend. 0 — Map: Hats, Teams, Bounties White hat: authorized defender/researcher. Black hat: criminal. Gray hat: unauthorized but claims good intent — still illegal, don't. Red team: authorized adversary emulation. Blue team: detect/respond/harden. Purple: both collaborate. Bug bounty: legal hacking inside a scope + rules (see HackerOne , Bugcrowd , GitHub Security Lab ). Start with OWASP Top 10 + OWASP Testing Guide . Papers to read (defensive lens): NIST SP 800 series (800-53, 800-115 testing) , MITRE ATT&CK (adversary tactics map), Cyber Kill Chain (Lockheed), NIST Incident Handling 800-61 . 1 — Lab, Not Real Life: Isolate Your Experiments Build a lab you can break without breaking law or others: Host: Debian/Ubuntu, updated, firewall on Hypervisor: VirtualBox (https://www.virtualbox.org/) or KVM/QEMU + virt-manager Net: Host-only / NAT, NO bridge to home LAN for vulnerable VMs Targets (vulnerable-by-design, local only): - Metasploitable 2/3 (https://github.com/rapid7/metasploitable3) - OWASP Juice Shop (https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop) - DVWA (https://github.com/digininja/DVWA) - WebGoat (https://github.com/WebGoat/WebGoat) Attacker: Kali Linux (https://www.kali.org/) as a toolbox, snapshots before/after Capture: Wireshark (https://www.wireshark.org/) on host-only only Snapshot everything. Lab firewall: vulnerable VMs must never reach internet. No real credentials, no real data, no scanning outside 192.168.56.0/24 lab range. Secure your lab: separate user, encrypted disk ( LUKS docs ), ufw deny incoming on host, VPN kill-switch if you must fetch tools, GPG-verify ISOs. 2 — How Attacks Are Structured (Kill Chain → ATT&CK, Defensive View) Recon → weaponize → deliver → exploit → install → command → act. Map each to ATT&CK tactics. Blue counters: harden, detect, segment, log, respond. Example: phishing (Initial Access) fails if MFA + user training + mail filtering win. Study NIST CSF : Govern/Identify/Protect/Detect/Respond/Recover. 3 — Recon & Scanning: What Attackers See, How Defenders Shrink It Concept: DNS, subdomains, ports, services, versions leak attack surface. Tools defenders use to audit own scope: Nmap ( nmap.org , github/nmap ), Amass ( owasp-amass ), theHarvester ( theHarvester ), Shodan ( shodan.io — defender search for own exposure). # LAB ONLY against your own VMs, e.g. 192.168.56.101: nmap -sV -O 192.168.56.101 # versions, OS guess — then YOU patch/hide them # Blue: close ports, least service, banner minimization, WAF/CDN in front Blue lesson: every open port/version you see, attacker sees. Inventory with Nmap , then firewall, update, segment. Log scans with Suricata / Snort . 4 — Web: The #1 Real-World Path (Understand → Fix) Learn OWASP Top 10 : injection, broken access control, XSS, SSRF, misconfig. Practice defensively on Juice Shop / DVWA locally; intercept with Burp Suite Community ( portswigger ) or OWASP ZAP ( zaproxy , github ). Defense pattern (the point): parameterize queries, ORM, allow-list validation ( Zod ), output-encode, CSP + HttpOnly/SameSite cookies via Helmet ( helmetjs ), strict access checks server-side, SSRF allow-lists + no cloud metadata access. Scan own code with Semgrep , deps with Grype . 5 — C Fundamentals: Stack, Memory, Why Safe Code Matters You don't need to exploit to defend — but you must grasp why memory bugs are critical. Theory only, lab only: // stack frame (simplified x86-64): high -> low // [args][ret addr][saved rbp][locals: char buf[64]] // Unsafe copy can overflow locals -> crash/hijack in theory. // Defense: -fstack-protector-strong -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 -Wl,-z,RelRO,-z,Now -fPIE -pie // + ASLR, NX, canaries, fuzzing, modern langs (Rust/Go) for new code. Learn safely: RPISEC MBE (course), pwn.college (ASU, lab + defense), awesome-pwn (curated learning) , papers: Smashing the Stack (Phrack 49, historic) — read as history + why mitigations exist. Practice defense: compile with protections, run ASan/UBSan , fuzz with AFL++ on your own code, verify with checksec / hardening-check . 6 — Passwords/Cracking: Why We Harden Auth (No Real Cracking) Concept: weak/reused passwords + no MFA = breach. Attackers use leaked lists + guessing in theory; your job is to make it fail : long unique passwords in KeePassXC ( keepassxc.org ), MFA everywhere (TOTP/WebAuthn), bcrypt/argon2 server-side, rate-limit + lockout, breach monitoring ( HIBP ). Audit own hashes in lab only with John ( openwall ) / Hashcat ( hashcat ) docs to prove policy works — never against others. 7 — Blue Team: Detect, Log, Respond Tools: Wireshark ( wireshark ) for packets, Suricata / Snort IDS, Wazuh ( wazuh , github ) SIEM, TheHive+Cortex ( TheHive ) case mgmt, Velociraptor ( velociraptor ) DFIR, Ghidra ( ghidra , NSA github ) for malware analysis in isolated VM . Playbooks: NIST 800-61 , SANS whitepapers . Log centrally, time-sync (NTP), alert on ATT&CK techniques you actually see in lab, rehearse restore from offline backups. Blue wins by preparation, not heroics. 8 — Bug Bounty Path (Legal Hacking Career) 1) Learn web + networking basics. 2) Lab: Juice Shop → PortSwigger Academy ( portswigger academy ). 3) Read scopes twice, respect out-of-scope, rate limits, disclosure rules. 4) Report: repro, impact, fix. Repos: OWASP WSTG checklist , HackTricks (defensive reference — use on own scope only) , PayloadsAllTheThings (test payloads for own lab/scope) . Never extort, never pivot beyond scope, never access real user data. 9 — Study Plan (6 Weeks, Lab + Defense) W1 Linux+networking + lab build. W2 OWASP Top 10 on Juice Shop + fix code. W3 Nmap/ZAP on own VMs + harden. W4 C/memory theory + compiler mitigations + fuzz own toy program. W5 Blue: Suricata+Wazuh alerts + IR drill. W6 Bounty-style report on lab target with fix PR. Throughout: ATT&CK mapping, write-ups, clean snapshots. Hack to protect. Learn stacks to build safer stacks. The best hacker on your network is the defender you trained.
